title: Band-aid Solutions
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Brien opens with the story of a torn meniscus that was treated with painkillers and rest until a specialist ordered an MRI and went after the root cause. He uses it as a lens on school device policy, arguing that schools too often cover symptoms in devices, behaviour, engagement and belonging rather than curing the underlying problem. Responding to Australia's November 2026 Digital Detox paper, he marshals screen-time data, an umbrella review of 23 meta-analyses, and a study of 26,000 Chinese students showing AI raised homework scores but lowered exam scores. He favours a blend of the NSW rule (screens only when better for learning than the alternative) and Victoria's explicit time caps, and he points out that 'limited' use is a vague instruction. His central claim is that limiting devices is only remission unless schools also have a clear behaviour curriculum and strong tier 1 instruction. The piece ends by insisting students still need to be taught to use digital tools well.
points: Brien's extended meniscus analogy frames device bans as symptom management that only holds if the root causes in behaviour, curriculum and instruction are also treated.
He cites a study of more than 26,000 Chinese students in which AI use lifted homework scores 18% yet cut monthly exam scores 20%, as evidence that performance is not learning.
He argues the vague word 'limited' in secondary device guidance can mean almost nothing, and prefers NSW's test of using screens only when better for learning than the alternative.
He notes that students who are digital natives still submit files named 'Document87.Docx', which undermines the digital literacy case for default device use.
His cure pairs reduced screen time with an embedded behaviour curriculum and quality tier 1 resources, plus explicit teaching of how to use the tools well.
quotes: The specialist looked for the root cause, then rather than simply treating the symptoms. This meant that rather than having brief relief followed by a return to pain and discomfort, I eventually moved to a state of being fully functional again.
Yet, in schools I have seen time and time again that so many issues are treated with band-aids to cover the symptoms rather than really addressing the underlying cause with a cure.

As we know performance does not equal learning. has previously warned us of the dangers of a beautifully kept notebook. Students using AI to complete their homework is the learning equivalent of having your coach run your long runs with your watch on for you in the lead up to a marathon. Sure, the runs happened, you’ve got the data to prove it. The data looks great too! Low heart rate, solid pace. The problem is, you didn’t do the work and the work is where learning lies.

Devices alone are not necessarily the problem but it is the cognitive outsourcing they provide through the pervasive nature of AI tools in all elements of digital infrastructure. Generative AI removes students need to think as they can just gain solutions to any question they post.

Limited is a tricky recommendation to make because it can mean everything and nothing. If a school currently has device use in every minute of the day, limited device use could mean that they do not have their device open for the first 5 minutes of the lesson. It could also mean that device use is completely abolished.

Additionally, a blanket ban or limit on device use serves no benefit if there are other underlying issues within the school around curriculum, behaviour, assessment or instruction. If a teacher has no capability to gain or reset attention with the class in front of them, then removing devices may improve attention a small amount, but chances are those students are still going to find distractions.

Unless schools have behaviour, instruction and curriculum at a high standard, limiting devices may alleviate some of the underlying symptoms, but it would be more like going into remission where the virus could eventually reactivate and spread.
